title: KMT Government Retreats to Taiwan
description: Following defeat in the Chinese Civil War, Chiang Kai-shek and roughly 1.2 million Nationalist troops, officials, and civilians fled to Taiwan, relocating the Republic of China government to Taipei. The ROC maintained its claim to be the legitimate government of all China, setting the foundational political and military tension that would define cross-strait relations for decades.

title: White Terror Begins Under Martial Law
description: Chiang Kai-shek declared martial law across Taiwan in May 1949, initiating what became known as the White Terror — a campaign of political repression targeting suspected communists, dissidents, and Taiwanese independence sympathizers. Tens of thousands were imprisoned or executed, with the period of martial law ultimately lasting until 1987, the longest in modern history.

title: Korean War Saves Taiwan: US 7th Fleet Deployed
description: After North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, President Truman ordered the US 7th Fleet into the Taiwan Strait, effectively blocking a planned PRC invasion of Taiwan. The intervention transformed Taiwan's strategic situation overnight, making it a frontline Cold War partner and beginning decades of US military and economic support.

title: US Military Aid and Economic Assistance Begins
description: The United States resumed military aid to the Republic of China and dispatched a Military Assistance Advisory Group to Taiwan following the Korean War outbreak. American economic assistance over the following decade totaled hundreds of millions of dollars, providing the capital foundation for Taiwan's subsequent export-led industrialization.

title: Land Reform Transforms Rural Economy
description: The KMT government completed a sweeping land-to-the-tiller reform program that redistributed farmland from landlords to tenant farmers, compensating landlords with industrial shares. The reform eliminated the old agrarian elite, created a class of smallholder farmers, and freed capital for industrial investment — widely credited as a key enabler of Taiwan's later economic miracle.

title: US-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty Signed
description: The United States and the Republic of China signed a Mutual Defense Treaty in December 1954, formalizing the American commitment to defend Taiwan against armed attack. The treaty anchored Taiwan within the US alliance system in the Pacific and remained the cornerstone of Taiwan's security until US derecognition in 1979.

title: First Taiwan Strait Crisis: PRC Bombards Quemoy
description: The People's Republic of China began intensive artillery bombardment of the Quemoy and Matsu islands held by ROC forces in September 1954, triggering the First Taiwan Strait Crisis. The United States responded by securing congressional authorization — the Formosa Resolution — to defend Taiwan and the offshore islands, and the crisis subsided after PRC bombardment halted in May 1955.

title: Second Taiwan Strait Crisis: Massive PRC Artillery Barrage
description: China launched a massive 44-day artillery bombardment of Quemoy beginning August 23, 1958, firing over 470,000 shells in the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis. The US deployed carrier battle groups and supplied Sidewinder missiles to Taiwan; the PRC eventually shifted to symbolic alternate-day shelling, which continued until 1979 when diplomatic normalization with the US ended the practice.

title: Lei Chen Arrested, Free China Movement Suppressed
description: Lei Chen, publisher of the influential Free China Fortnightly magazine and organizer of an opposition party, was arrested and sentenced to ten years in prison on charges of harboring a communist spy. The crackdown eliminated the most significant challenge to KMT one-party rule of the 1950s and demonstrated the limits of political liberalization under Chiang Kai-shek.

title: US Economic Aid Program Ends: Taiwan Graduates
description: The United States formally terminated its economic aid program to Taiwan in 1965, reflecting the island's successful development trajectory that no longer required external capital injections. Taiwan was one of the first US aid recipients to graduate from the program, signaling its transformation into a middle-income economy and a model for export-led development.

title: Export Processing Zones Established at Kaohsiung
description: Taiwan established its first Export Processing Zone at Kaohsiung in 1966, creating a dedicated manufacturing enclave with tax incentives and streamlined customs procedures to attract foreign investment. The zones became a template for East Asian industrial development and drove Taiwan's transformation into a major electronics and textiles exporter throughout the 1970s.

title: ROC Expelled from United Nations; PRC Takes Seat
description: The United Nations General Assembly passed Resolution 2758 in October 1971, recognizing the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate representative of China and expelling the Republic of China delegation. The ROC's loss of its UN Security Council seat was a devastating diplomatic blow, beginning Taiwan's decades-long international isolation and the erosion of its formal diplomatic recognition.

title: Nixon-Mao Shanghai Communique Undermines Taiwan
description: President Nixon's historic visit to China produced the Shanghai Communique of February 1972, in which the United States acknowledged the Chinese position that there is one China and Taiwan is part of China, without explicitly endorsing it. The statement began the process of diplomatic normalization that would culminate in 1979, leaving Taiwan in a fundamentally weakened international position.

title: Ten Major Construction Projects Launch Industrial Scale-Up
description: Premier Chiang Ching-kuo launched the Ten Major Construction Projects in 1973 — a state-led infrastructure and heavy industry program including nuclear plants, steel mills, petrochemical plants, and a north-south freeway. The initiative transformed Taiwan's industrial base from light manufacturing to capital-intensive sectors and positioned the island for the technology leap of the 1980s.

title: Chiang Kai-shek Dies After 26 Years in Power
description: Chiang Kai-shek died in Taipei on April 5, 1975, ending an era of authoritarian rule that had simultaneously suppressed political opposition and overseen dramatic economic development. His death elevated Vice President Yen Chia-kan to the presidency while Chiang Ching-kuo consolidated control as KMT party chairman and premier, setting the stage for a partial opening of political space.

title: Chiang Ching-kuo Elected President
description: Chiang Ching-kuo was elected president of the Republic of China in 1978 by the National Assembly, consolidating his position as Taiwan's paramount leader following the death of his father. Though initially continuing authoritarian rule, Chiang Ching-kuo would prove to be a transitional figure who ultimately authorized the lifting of martial law and tolerated growing political pluralism.

title: US Derecognizes Taiwan, Establishes Relations with PRC
description: The United States formally switched diplomatic recognition from the Republic of China to the People's Republic of China on January 1, 1979, abrogating the Mutual Defense Treaty and withdrawing its ambassador from Taipei. The derecognition was Taiwan's worst diplomatic crisis, though Congress simultaneously passed the Taiwan Relations Act to maintain de facto relations and arms sales.

title: Taiwan Relations Act Passes US Congress
description: The Taiwan Relations Act, signed by President Carter in April 1979, established the American Institute in Taiwan as a de facto embassy and committed the US to provide Taiwan with defensive arms and to treat any attempt to determine Taiwan's future by non-peaceful means as a matter of grave concern. The act became the legal framework for US-Taiwan relations and a partial substitute for the terminated defense treaty.

title: Kaohsiung Incident: Democracy Movement Watershed
description: On December 10, 1979 — International Human Rights Day — opposition activists organizing around Formosa Magazine held a rally in Kaohsiung that was violently suppressed by security forces, resulting in mass arrests of virtually the entire democratic opposition leadership including Annette Lu and Chen Shui-bian's mentor Huang Hsin-chieh. The subsequent military tribunals, held partly in public at opposition insistence, created national sympathy for the democracy movement and its lawyers became the next generation of opposition leaders.

title: Lin Family Murders Shock Democratic Movement
description: The wife and twin daughters of jailed democracy activist Lin Yi-hsiung were stabbed to death in their home in February 1980 while under police surveillance, in a crime that was never officially solved. The murders galvanized public sympathy for the democratic opposition and were widely attributed to security services, becoming a defining moment in Taiwan's democratization narrative.

title: TSMC Founder Morris Chang Joins Industrial Technology Research Institute
description: Morris Chang, who would later found TSMC, joined Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute as president in 1985, but the semiconductor ambitions began taking shape in the late 1970s-early 1980s when government planners identified semiconductors as a strategic industry. State investment in electronics R&D through ITRI laid the institutional groundwork for Taiwan's eventual dominance in chip manufacturing.

title: Henry Liu (Deng Nan-jung) Assassination in California
description: Taiwan-born US citizen Henry Liu, who had written a critical biography of Chiang Ching-kuo, was murdered in his California home in October 1984 by agents of Taiwan's Defense Intelligence Bureau acting on orders from Taipei. The assassination caused a major diplomatic crisis with the United States and led to the conviction of Taiwan intelligence officers, revealing the reach of KMT repression beyond Taiwan's borders.

title: Democratic Progressive Party Founded Illegally
description: A group of opposition politicians formed the Democratic Progressive Party in September 1986 without the required government authorization — an act that technically violated martial law restrictions on new political parties. Chiang Ching-kuo chose not to prosecute, tacitly permitting the DPP's existence and signaling the beginning of Taiwan's transition to multi-party democracy.

title: Martial Law Lifted After 38 Years
description: President Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law on July 15, 1987, ending the longest continuous period of martial law in modern history at 38 years and 57 days. The lifting legalized new political parties, relaxed press restrictions, and permitted mainlander veterans to visit relatives in China for the first time, marking the decisive turning point in Taiwan's democratization.

title: Taiwan Opens Cross-Strait Family Visits to Mainland
description: Following the lifting of martial law, Taiwan allowed its citizens — particularly the mainlanders who had come over with the KMT in 1949 — to visit relatives in the People's Republic of China for the first time. The opening initiated the gradual normalization of cross-strait social and economic contact that would eventually grow into massive trade and investment flows.

title: TSMC Founded: World's First Pure-Play Foundry
description: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company was established in 1987 with government backing and Morris Chang as chairman, pioneering the pure-play foundry model that manufactured chips for other companies' designs rather than competing in finished products. TSMC's business model proved transformative for the global semiconductor industry, enabling the fabless chip design industry and eventually making Taiwan the world's most critical chokepoint in advanced chip production.

title: Lee Teng-hui Becomes First Taiwanese-Born President
description: Following Chiang Ching-kuo's death in January 1988, Vice President Lee Teng-hui was sworn in as president — the first native Taiwanese-born leader of the Republic of China. Lee's ascension represented a dramatic shift from mainlander KMT dominance and he would go on to lead Taiwan's full democratic transition, earning the title 'Father of Taiwan's democracy.'

title: Press Law Revised, Newspapers Liberalized
description: Taiwan revised its press regulations in 1989, lifting bans on new newspaper licenses and ending restrictions on newspaper page counts that had limited press pluralism for decades. The liberalization of media, combined with political party legalization, rapidly transformed Taiwan's information environment and created a vibrant if contentious press.

title: ROC Formally Ends State of War with PRC
description: Taiwan's National Assembly formally terminated the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion in April 1991, officially ending the state of civil war with the People's Republic of China that had technically persisted since 1949. The act was a significant step in normalizing cross-strait relations and also enabled major constitutional reforms.

title: First Full Legislative Yuan Elections Held
description: Taiwan held the first fully competitive elections for all Legislative Yuan seats in December 1992, replacing the aging mainland-era legislators who had held their seats since 1947 without facing the electorate. The KMT won a majority but the DPP made substantial gains, marking the effective beginning of Taiwan's fully competitive legislative politics.

title: 1992 Consensus on Cross-Strait Relations
description: Talks between Taiwan's Straits Exchange Foundation and China's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits produced what became known as the '1992 Consensus' — an ambiguous agreement that both sides acknowledge one China while agreeing to disagree on what one China means. The consensus became a contested cornerstone of cross-strait diplomacy, accepted by the KMT and rejected by the DPP as a legitimate framework.

title: Koo-Wang Talks: First Official Cross-Strait Negotiations
description: The first official cross-strait talks between SEF Chairman Koo Chen-fu and ARATS Chairman Wang Daohan took place in Singapore in April 1993, marking the highest-level formal contact between the two sides since 1949. The talks produced four agreements on practical matters including document authentication, creating a framework for subsequent cross-strait dialogue.

title: Taiwan Launches 'Go South' Economic Policy
description: Taiwan introduced the Southward Policy in 1994, offering incentives for Taiwanese businesses to invest in Southeast Asia as an alternative to growing economic dependence on mainland China. The policy reflected strategic anxiety about over-concentration in the mainland market and was periodically reinvigorated in subsequent decades, especially under DPP administrations.

title: Lee Teng-hui Visits Cornell University
description: President Lee Teng-hui made a private visit to Cornell University in June 1995, becoming the first sitting ROC president to visit the United States since 1978 derecognition. Beijing viewed the visit as a move toward formal independence, triggering the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis, and temporarily recalled its US ambassador in protest.

title: Third Taiwan Strait Crisis: PRC Missile Tests
description: The People's Republic of China conducted a series of missile tests and large-scale military exercises in waters close to Taiwan beginning in July 1995 and continuing into 1996, in response to Lee Teng-hui's US visit and his perceived push for independence. The crisis was the most serious cross-strait military confrontation since 1958 and prompted the United States to deploy two aircraft carrier battle groups to the region.

title: First Direct Presidential Election: Lee Teng-hui Wins
description: Taiwan held its first direct popular presidential election on March 23, 1996, with incumbent Lee Teng-hui winning 54 percent of the vote amid continued PRC missile tests and military exercises designed to intimidate voters. The election was a historic milestone in democratic consolidation, and the PRC's intimidation tactics appeared to backfire by rallying public support for Lee.

title: US Carrier Groups Deter PRC During Strait Crisis
description: The United States deployed two aircraft carrier battle groups — the USS Independence and USS Nimitz — to the Taiwan Strait region in March 1996 during the peak of the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis. The deployment was the largest US show of force in Asia since the Vietnam War and effectively deterred further PRC escalation, reaffirming the credibility of American security commitments to Taiwan.

title: Taiwan Economy Weathers Asian Financial Crisis
description: While much of East and Southeast Asia suffered devastating currency crises in 1997, Taiwan's economy proved comparatively resilient due to its large foreign exchange reserves, limited short-term foreign debt, and diversified export base in electronics. Taiwan's managed float of the New Taiwan Dollar limited contagion and the island emerged from the crisis without an IMF bailout — a point of national pride.

title: Major Earthquake Kills 2,400 in Central Taiwan
description: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near the town of Chi-chi in central Taiwan on September 21, 1999, killing approximately 2,400 people, injuring over 10,000, and leaving 100,000 homeless. The disaster was Taiwan's deadliest earthquake in 70 years and tested the government's emergency response capabilities; international aid including from the US and Japan was mobilized.

title: Lee Teng-hui's Two-States Theory Provokes Beijing
description: President Lee Teng-hui declared in a radio interview in July 1999 that cross-strait relations should be characterized as a 'special state-to-state relationship,' effectively framing Taiwan as a separate state rather than a renegade province. Beijing responded furiously, suspending cross-strait dialogue and issuing military warnings, and the statement contributed to PRC support for Lee's defeat in the 2000 election.

title: Chen Shui-bian Wins Presidency: First DPP Victory
description: Democratic Progressive Party candidate Chen Shui-bian won the presidential election on March 18, 2000, becoming the first non-KMT president in ROC history and completing Taiwan's first democratic transfer of power between parties. Chen received 39 percent of the vote in a three-way race, with the KMT split between official candidate Lien Chan and popular former Taiwan Governor James Soong.

title: Taiwan Joins World Trade Organization
description: Taiwan acceded to the World Trade Organization in January 2001 as the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu — one day after the People's Republic of China. WTO membership formalized Taiwan's integration into the rules-based global trading order and required significant domestic economic liberalization, though the PRC had insisted Taiwan join under a name that did not imply statehood.

title: Chen Shui-bian's 'One Country on Each Side' Statement
description: President Chen Shui-bian stated in August 2002 that Taiwan and China are 'one country on each side' of the strait, explicitly rejecting the one-China framework and asserting Taiwan's de facto independent statehood. The statement alarmed Washington as well as Beijing, with the US privately cautioning Chen against provocative statements that could trigger a military crisis.

title: SARS Outbreak Hits Taiwan Hard
description: Taiwan experienced a severe outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome in 2003, with 346 confirmed cases and 73 deaths — concentrated in the Taipei region and particularly a quarantine cluster at Hoping Hospital. The outbreak exposed weaknesses in Taiwan's public health infrastructure and led to subsequent reforms in epidemic response capacity.

title: Chen Shui-bian Re-elected After Assassination Attempt
description: President Chen Shui-bian narrowly won re-election on March 20, 2004, by approximately 30,000 votes out of 13 million cast, one day after he and Vice President Lu Hsiu-lien were grazed by bullets in a drive-by shooting whose circumstances remained disputed. The opposition KMT-PFP alliance disputed the result and the shooting's authenticity, leading to prolonged political turmoil.

title: China's Anti-Secession Law Threatens Force Against Taiwan
description: The People's Republic of China enacted the Anti-Secession Law in March 2005, formally codifying Beijing's legal basis for using 'non-peaceful means' against Taiwan if it declared independence or if peaceful reunification became impossible. The law was the first time China explicitly legislated a legal trigger for military action, generating strong protests from Taiwan and concern in Washington.

title: Cross-Strait Charter Flights Begin for Lunar New Year
description: Taiwan and China operated direct charter flights across the strait during Lunar New Year 2005 for the first time since 1949, with dozens of flights carrying tens of thousands of Taiwanese businesspeople and their families. The flights were a symbolic milestone in cross-strait normalization even though regular direct links remained years away.

title: Chen Shui-bian Corruption Scandal Paralyzes Government
description: Revelations that President Chen's wife Wu Shu-jen had misused a state affairs fund triggered massive street protests organized by former DPP ally Shih Ming-teh demanding Chen's resignation in 2006. Though Chen survived through his term, the corruption scandal severely damaged the DPP's credibility and set the stage for a sweeping KMT electoral comeback in 2008.

title: Ma Ying-jeou Wins Presidency: KMT Returns to Power
description: KMT candidate Ma Ying-jeou won the presidential election in March 2008 with 58 percent of the vote, ending eight years of DPP rule and initiating a period of significant cross-strait rapprochement. Ma's victory was also accompanied by a KMT legislative supermajority, giving the party dominant control over Taiwan's government.

title: Direct Cross-Strait Flights, Shipping, and Mail Links Opened
description: Taiwan and China implemented the 'three links' — direct air, sea, and postal links — in December 2008 after 60 years of separation, dramatically reducing travel and shipping times between the two sides. The opening enabled a rapid expansion of Taiwanese investment and tourism to the mainland, deepening economic interdependence.

title: Cross-Strait Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement Negotiations Begin
description: Taiwan and China began negotiations on the Cross-Strait Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA) in 2009, seeking to reduce tariffs and normalize trade flows. The ECFA was eventually signed in 2010, the most significant economic agreement between the two sides, but its expansion into services provoked the 2014 Sunflower Movement.

title: ECFA Signed: Landmark Cross-Strait Trade Agreement
description: Taiwan and China signed the Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement in June 2010, reducing tariffs on hundreds of goods and services and establishing a framework for continued trade liberalization. ECFA was politically controversial in Taiwan — supporters argued it was economically necessary, critics warned of dangerous economic dependence on the mainland.

title: Ma Ying-jeou Re-elected, Cross-Strait Ties Continue
description: President Ma Ying-jeou won a second term in January 2012, defeating DPP candidate Tsai Ing-wen by 51 to 45 percent, with cross-strait relations and economic policy as central issues. Ma's re-election signaled continued public support for engagement with China, though Tsai's strong showing indicated growing DPP competitiveness on national issues.

title: Cross-Strait Services Trade Agreement Signed
description: Taiwan and China signed the Cross-Strait Services Trade Agreement in June 2013, extending ECFA's framework to the services sector and allowing Chinese companies to invest in Taiwanese service industries. The agreement proved politically toxic in Taiwan; its secretive negotiation process and perceived risks to Taiwanese workers and small businesses fueled the 2014 Sunflower Movement.

title: Sunflower Movement Occupies Legislature Against Services Pact
description: Thousands of students and civil society activists occupied Taiwan's Legislative Yuan for 24 days beginning March 18, 2014, protesting the legislative fast-tracking of the Cross-Strait Services Trade Agreement without proper committee review. The Sunflower Movement galvanized a generation of Taiwanese civic consciousness, blocked the services agreement, and helped launch a new civic political movement that fed into the DPP's 2016 landslide.

title: Hong Kong Umbrella Movement Deepens Taiwan-China Divide
description: Hong Kong's Umbrella Movement — demanding genuine universal suffrage — ran from September to December 2014 and was closely watched in Taiwan as a test of Beijing's willingness to honor its 'one country, two systems' promises. The movement's failure strengthened Taiwanese skepticism about any reunification framework that relied on Beijing's good faith.

title: Xi-Ma Summit in Singapore: First Cross-Strait Leader Meeting
description: Taiwan's President Ma Ying-jeou and China's President Xi Jinping met in Singapore on November 7, 2015, the first meeting between the leaders of the two sides since 1949. The summit was largely symbolic with no agreements signed, but it was a historic milestone in cross-strait relations, though it failed to improve Ma's domestic standing before the 2016 elections.

title: Tsai Ing-wen Elected: First Female President, DPP Majority
description: Democratic Progressive Party candidate Tsai Ing-wen won the presidential election on January 16, 2016 with 56 percent of the vote, becoming Taiwan's first female president, while the DPP simultaneously won a legislative majority for the first time. Tsai's victory represented a decisive rejection of Ma's cross-strait engagement policy and reflected a generational shift in Taiwanese identity.

title: Beijing Suspends Cross-Strait Dialogue After Tsai Election
description: China suspended official cross-strait dialogue through the SEF-ARATS mechanism after Tsai Ing-wen's election in 2016, citing her refusal to explicitly endorse the 1992 Consensus and one-China framework. The suspension effectively froze institutionalized cross-strait communication and increased tensions, with Beijing also stepping up military pressure in the form of more frequent PLA air and naval operations near Taiwan.

title: Taiwan Launches New Southbound Policy
description: President Tsai Ing-wen launched the New Southbound Policy in 2016, providing government resources and incentives to diversify Taiwan's economic ties toward Southeast Asia, South Asia, Australia, and New Zealand as an alternative to mainland China dependence. The policy was a strategic response to cross-strait tensions and sought to reduce Taiwan's economic vulnerability to Chinese pressure.

title: Panama Breaks Ties with Taiwan, Recognizes PRC
description: Panama switched diplomatic recognition from the Republic of China to the People's Republic of China in June 2017, beginning a wave of Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies defecting to Beijing under Xi Jinping's more assertive cross-strait policy. Taiwan's formal diplomatic allies fell from 22 to approximately 13 over Tsai's first term, as China systematically picked off Taiwan's remaining partners.

title: PLA Air Force Begins Regular Median Line Crossings
description: China's People's Liberation Army Air Force began conducting regular incursions across the median line of the Taiwan Strait in 2018, a de facto boundary that had been largely respected since the 1950s. The crossings escalated further in subsequent years, with dozens of PLA aircraft entering Taiwan's Air Defense Identification Zone in single days, dramatically increasing Taiwan's air force scrambling costs.

title: Hong Kong's National Security Law Collapses 'One Country, Two Systems' Credibility
description: The mass protests in Hong Kong beginning in June 2019 against a proposed extradition bill, and Beijing's subsequent imposition of a sweeping National Security Law in 2020, devastated the credibility of 'one country, two systems' as a framework for Taiwan's potential reunification. Taiwan's public opinion hardened sharply against any form of unification, providing Tsai Ing-wen with a major political boost heading into her 2020 re-election campaign.

title: Taiwan Legalizes Same-Sex Marriage
description: Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed a law legalizing same-sex marriage on May 17, 2019, making Taiwan the first Asian jurisdiction to do so. The landmark legislation followed a Constitutional Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights and came despite referendum results the previous year that showed majority opposition, representing a significant expansion of civil rights.

title: Tsai Ing-wen Re-elected in Landslide Amid Hong Kong Crisis
description: President Tsai Ing-wen won re-election on January 11, 2020 with a record 8.17 million votes and 57 percent of the ballot, the largest vote total in Taiwan's democratic history. Her landslide was driven by public anger at Beijing's treatment of Hong Kong protesters, Taiwan's strong economic performance, and a successful defense against Chinese disinformation campaigns.

title: Taiwan's COVID-19 Response Wins International Praise
description: Taiwan achieved one of the world's most effective early responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, with rapid border controls, mask production scaling, digital contact tracing, and proactive quarantine measures that kept infections extremely low through 2020 and 2021. Taiwan's success attracted international attention and renewed calls for Taiwan's inclusion in the World Health Organization, which Beijing blocked.

title: Global Chip Shortage Elevates TSMC's Strategic Centrality
description: The COVID-19 pandemic-induced global semiconductor shortage of 2020-2021 exposed the world's dependence on Taiwan's chip manufacturing ecosystem, with TSMC producing over 90 percent of the world's most advanced chips. The crisis triggered a geopolitical awakening about Taiwan's irreplaceable role in global technology supply chains and accelerated US, European, and Japanese efforts to attract TSMC manufacturing investments.

title: TSMC Begins Arizona Fabrication Plant Construction
description: TSMC announced and began construction of a $12 billion fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona in 2021, responding to US government pressure and financial incentives to diversify advanced chip production outside Taiwan. The investment — later expanded to over $65 billion — was the largest foreign direct investment in US history and reflected the growing strategic importance of semiconductor supply chain resilience.

title: PLA Conducts Record Air Incursions into Taiwan ADIZ
description: China's PLA Air Force conducted unprecedented incursions into Taiwan's Air Defense Identification Zone throughout 2021, with a record single-day incursion of 56 aircraft in October. The increased frequency and scale of operations — totaling hundreds of sorties for the year — was designed to normalize PLA military presence around Taiwan and test Taiwanese and US resolve.

title: Pelosi Visit Triggers Unprecedented PLA Encirclement Drills
description: US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan on August 2-3, 2022 was the highest-profile American official visit since 1997 and triggered the largest PLA military exercises around Taiwan since 1996, including missile salvos that landed in Japan's exclusive economic zone. China's five-day encirclement exercises simulated a blockade and demonstrated the PLA's ability to conduct multi-domain operations around Taiwan.

title: US CHIPS and Science Act Incentivizes Taiwan Semiconductor Diversification
description: The United States enacted the CHIPS and Science Act in August 2022, providing $52 billion in subsidies to incentivize semiconductor manufacturing in the US and limiting recipients from expanding advanced chip production in China. The act was designed in significant part to reduce US dependence on Taiwan-produced chips and attracted additional TSMC investment commitments.

title: Taiwan Loses More Diplomatic Allies to PRC
description: Honduras switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in March 2023, continuing the systematic erosion of Taiwan's formal diplomatic allies under sustained Chinese financial pressure. By mid-decade Taiwan's formal allies numbered approximately 12, confined largely to small Pacific island nations, Caribbean states, and the Holy See.

title: Taiwan Defense Budget Hits Record as Military Threat Grows
description: Taiwan approved its largest defense budget in history in 2023, with spending exceeding NT$610 billion (approximately $19 billion) as the government responded to escalating PLA military pressure with extended conscription terms and accelerated weapons procurement. The shift reflected a significant rethinking of Taiwan's defense strategy toward a more credible deterrence posture.

title: William Lai Selected as DPP Presidential Candidate
description: Vice President William Lai Ching-te, who had previously expressed more explicit pro-independence views than President Tsai, won the DPP primary in 2023 to become the party's presidential candidate. Lai's selection alarmed Beijing, which had previously labeled him a 'troublemaker' and 'Taiwan independence worker,' raising the geopolitical stakes of the upcoming 2024 election.

title: Lai Ching-te Wins Presidency; KMT Makes Legislative Gains
description: William Lai Ching-te of the DPP won the presidential election on January 13, 2024 with approximately 40 percent of the vote in a three-way race, becoming Taiwan's new president, though the DPP lost its legislative majority with the opposition KMT and TPP combining to control the legislature. Lai's victory was the third consecutive DPP presidential win but his minority government faced a politically divided legislature.

title: Major Earthquake Strikes Hualien, Killing Dozens
description: A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck offshore Hualien on the east coast of Taiwan on April 3, 2024, the island's strongest in 25 years, killing at least 13 people, injuring hundreds, and causing significant structural damage in Hualien city and surrounding mountain areas. TSMC's operations in nearby Tainan were briefly disrupted but quickly restored, highlighting the semiconductor industry's earthquake vulnerability.

title: PRC Launches Military Drills After Lai Ching-te Inauguration
description: China launched two days of large-scale military exercises surrounding Taiwan in May 2024, code-named Joint Sword-2024A, immediately following President Lai Ching-te's inauguration speech, which Beijing characterized as separatist. The exercises involved PLA Army, Navy, Air Force, Rocket Force, and Coast Guard units in a simulated blockade, representing a further escalation of China's coercive military signaling.
